response.query: What sample-size or precision estimates are needed to detect clinically meaningful changes in rare, high-severity events and what alternative analyses for sparse events are recommended?
response.answer: To detect clinically meaningful changes in rare, high-severity events, large sample sizes or rare event simulation models are needed; alternative analyses like Poisson regression or rare event-focused machine learning techniques are recommended.

results.title: Quantitative Phase Imaging XII, Conference Details
results.content: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) of live-cells delivers improved label-free contrast and enhanced cell phenotype analysis; however, live-cell QPI is difficult for many biologists to implement due to the complexity and limited throughput of current QPI based approaches. Quantitative phase imaging (QPI), and its three-dimensional analogue, holotomography, permit label-free measurements of the biophysical state of single cells with extreme precision. Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is a vital technique in biology and medicine, enabling label-free microscopic analysis of living cells and transparent specimens. The classification or segmentation of cells from quantitative phase imaging (QPI) measurements enables studies of cell function and behavior, disease progression and prognosis, high-throughput and automated analyses, and drug development. Label-free high-content analysis at the single cell level utilizing artificial neural network supported correlative bright field imaging and digital holographic quantitative phase microscopy. This work presents a comprehensive approach to quantitative, label-free 3D imaging and analysis of live cells and organoids, leveraging digital holographic tomography and advanced computational reconstruction techniques.

results.title: Occupational Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica
results.content: OSHA believes that if the most recent cost estimates had been used, they would have had a minor effect on Inforum's estimate of the employment impact of the final rule. OSHA used the exposure-response models from these studies in a life table analysis to estimate excess risk of disease mortality from exposure to respirable crystalline silica after accounting for competing causes of death due to background causes. Section 6(b)(5) of the OSH Act states: “The Secretary, in promulgating standards dealing with toxic materials or harmful physical agents under this subsection, shall set the standard which most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, on the basis of the best available evidence, that no employee will suffer material impairment of health or functional capacity even if such employee has regular exposure to the hazard dealt with by such standard for the period of his working life.” Given that OSHA must analyze significant risk over a working life, the Agency estimated benefits for the affected population over the same period.
